ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry (eating disorders) Consultation — Elisabeth of Austria — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: One-week medical stabilization check and eating disorders psychiatry consultation

text.paragraph: Weight loss to a BMI of 16.0 with fatigue, ankle swelling, dizziness on standing and a slow pulse in a 56-year-old woman with restrictive eating, frequent self-weighing and hours of daily exercise since early adulthood, and recurrent depression with grief. Please confirm the diagnosis, advise on the level of care and on restarting nutrition safely, and lead a multidisciplinary plan that she can follow while she travels and that protects her privacy. [S]

list.item: Is this anorexia nervosa, another specified feeding or eating disorder, or a medical illness, in a woman of 56 whose restriction began in early adulthood?
Can she be treated as an outpatient, and what findings should lead to admission?
How should nutrition be advanced, given her refeeding risk, and how should she be monitored?
What psychological treatment and team do you recommend, given her travel and her need for privacy?
How should her depression, grief and passive thoughts of death be treated alongside the eating disorder, and when should an antidepressant start?
What should be done about her exercise and her bones?

text.paragraph: Empress Elisabeth, 56, is seen at the request of Dr. Marchetti-Osei. Since her late teens she has restricted her eating, with single-food meals, a fixed upper weight of 50 kg that she has kept below for decades, tight lacing, and four to six hours of fast walking a day with gymnastics each morning; she feels anxious and guilty if she cannot exercise. She weighs herself up to three times a day. Over six months she has lost about 6 kg, and she has become tired, cold, dizzy on standing and swollen at the ankles. She describes an intense fear of gaining weight and sees herself as larger than she is, though she accepts that she is too thin. She denies binge eating, vomiting, laxatives, diuretics or diet pills. Her mood has been low for years, worse since the death of her son five years ago, a bereavement by suicide; she has passive thoughts of being better off dead without intent, plan or past attempts. She has had a week of the meal plan and thiamine, missed the blood test planned for three to four days, and has walked about two hours a day. She travels constantly and fears that her illness will become public. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Elisabeth Amalie Eugenie, Duchess in Bavaria, called Sisi, was born on December 24, 1837, in Munich, the daughter of Duke Max in Bavaria and Duchess Ludovika. [D]
She married her cousin, Emperor Franz Joseph I, on April 24, 1854, in the Augustinerkirche in Vienna, and became Empress of Austria and, later, Queen of Hungary. She had four children. [D]

From about 1859 she was reported to suffer from a mysterious illness, with cough, poor nutrition, anemia and exhaustion; she spent the winter of 1860 to 1861 on Madeira and, after a relapse, four months on Corfu, and recovered quickly whenever she travelled. [D]
At 1.72 m she was unusually tall for a woman of her time, with an extremely slender figure. [D]

Through her life she followed many diets; for periods each meal was a single food, such as egg, a milk product, orange or broth, and her 'magic weight' was fifty kilos. In her last years she weighed herself up to three times a day, and in 1894 she weighed as little as 43.5 kg, a body mass index of about 14.7 at her height. [D]
Her waist measured only about 50 cm at its smallest, in tightly laced corsets and dresses sewn around it. [D]

She hiked for hours every day and had exercise rooms installed in her apartments; in the Vienna Hofburg the wall bars, high bar and rings are preserved, and she had a large gymnasium with heavy apparatus. She was one of the best horsewomen in Europe, but gave up riding at the beginning of the 1880s because of health problems. [D]

A psychiatrist's biographical essay writes that in her last years she was increasingly troubled by her undernutrition, with fluid accumulation in the body and severe bodily pains, and that she was diagnosed with chlorosis. [D]
Eating-disorder researchers write that she sometimes suffered from edema as a consequence of severe starvation. [R]

A Swiss newspaper reported in 2024 that letters kept by her spa physician at Bad Kissingen, found in the city archive, describe complaints including rheumatic attacks, sciatica, joint pain and hunger edema at the ankles. [D]

Psychiatrists and eating-disorder researchers have argued that she met the criteria for anorexia nervosa: one essay states that 'without doubt' she qualified, a German study describes fasting rituals, gymnastics, hours of riding, forced marches and a considerable fear of weight gain, and Hungarian researchers describe many features of anorexia nervosa and suggest it was closely related to depression. [R]

On January 30, 1889, her son, Crown Prince Rudolf, born in 1858, was found dead with a young woman at the Mayerling hunting lodge; historians regard as certain only that he killed her and then himself. [D]

It is said that her son's death prompted her to wear only mourning from then on. She suffered from ever-deepening depressions, which in her last years are thought to have developed into a kind of death-wish. [D]

After her son's death she sought to master her inner unrest with extended travels and a retreat to Corfu, where she had the Achilleion, a palatial villa, built; she lost interest in it once it was finished and left the island six years after its completion. She often travelled incognito. [D]

tr.td: Weight loss to a body mass index of 16.0 (47.4 kg at 172 cm), about 6 kg over six months, with fatigue, swelling of both ankles, dizziness on standing, slow pulse and cold intolerance; cause not established at intake; a restrictive eating disorder suspected, with thyroid disease, celiac disease, diabetes, malignancy and adrenal insufficiency to be excluded; eating disorders psychiatry consultation requested
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to her documented restrictive eating, low weight and swelling; superseded by the diagnosis at the consultation.

Anorexia nervosa, restricting type, moderate (DSM-5-TR), with compulsive exercise and frequent self-weighing, beginning in early adulthood; complicated at diagnosis by sinus bradycardia, orthostatic dizziness, ankle edema, mild anemia and leukopenia, low glucose, raised ALT and low phosphate after refeeding began
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation, linked to her documented restrictive eating and exercise and to the retrospective diagnosis of anorexia nervosa (R).
Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate, with persistent grief for her son, who died five years ago; passive thoughts of death without intent or plan at intake
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis linked to her documented mourning and ever-deepening depressions; not a claim that she was so diagnosed.

code.displayName: Relevant Diagnostic Tests and/or Laboratory Data

list.item: Anorexia nervosa, restricting type, moderate (DSM-5-TR) (F50.011). Restriction leading to a significantly low weight, intense fear of weight gain with persistent behavior that prevents it, and a disturbed experience of her body meet the DSM-5-TR criteria for anorexia nervosa; with no binge eating or purging in the last three months it is the restricting type, and a BMI of 16.0 at intake is moderate. OSFED does not apply because all criteria are met. Most anorexia nervosa in later life, as here, began in youth and became long-standing. The normal TSH, CRP, celiac antibody and electrolytes, with low rather than high glucose, make thyroid disease, inflammation, celiac disease, diabetes and adrenal insufficiency unlikely; no further tests are needed. Compulsive exercise is part of the disorder. [S]

Level of care and refeeding. She does not meet the thresholds for admission: her pulse is above 40 awake, systolic pressure above 90, temperature above 35.6 C, potassium above 3.0 mmol/L, and she is eating. Admission would be advised for any of those, for fainting, chest pain or arrhythmia, phosphate below 2.0 mg/dL, a fall in weight despite treatment, or food refusal. Her phosphate of 2.3 mg/dL is an early refeeding effect that needs replacement and weekly checks. The slightly worse ankle edema is refeeding edema; a diuretic would worsen it later. [S]

Recurrent depression with persistent grief (F33.1). A recurrent moderate depressive episode with persistent grief, bereavement by suicide, and passive thoughts of death without intent or plan. Antidepressants work poorly at very low weight and starvation mimics depression, so nutrition comes first; an SSRI with low QT risk, such as sertraline, is reasonable once nutrition is under way and the ECG is repeated. [S]

Bones and exercise. Decades of low weight and her age put her at high risk of low bone mass; DXA is indicated. Weight restoration is the main treatment. Exercise should be limited while her pulse and blood pressure are abnormal. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Marchetti-Osei's intake note, ECG and tests (sinus bradycardia 52, QTc 438 ms; hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, white cells 3.4 x10^3/uL, glucose 68 mg/dL, ALT 52 U/L, TSH 2.2 mIU/L, CRP 1.0 mg/L, tissue transglutaminase IgA negative, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL). Today, seven days into the meal plan: sodium 137, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, phosphate 2.3 mg/dL, magnesium 1.8 mg/dL, glucose 74 mg/dL. Weight 47.9 kg, BMI 16.2. [S]

list.item: Outpatient treatment: weekly weights at therapy, weekly blood tests for three weeks, and medical review by Dr. Marchetti-Osei in three weeks and at least every two months while underweight; admission for any of the thresholds above. [S]
Phosphorus 250 mg twice daily for three weeks; finish 14 days of thiamine; electrolytes, phosphate and magnesium weekly for three weeks, then at each visit while underweight. [S]
The dietitian to advance the meal plan by about 200 to 300 kcal every few days toward weight gain of 0.5 to 1 kg a week, with three meals and two to three snacks. [S]

Weekly enhanced cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-E) with open weighing in the session, and an end to weighing at home; video sessions when she travels; psychiatry review by video at about four weeks and then as needed. [S]
No gymnastics and walks of no more than an hour a day for now, with a graded return agreed by the team once vital signs are normal and weight is rising. [S]

Sertraline 25 mg, then 50 mg, at about four weeks if the ECG is normal, with grief-focused work in therapy; safety review at every visit and the safety plan kept current, including crisis numbers abroad. [S]
DXA of the spine and hip at about four weeks, with calcium to about 1,200 mg a day and vitamin D. [S]
Privacy: a restricted chart, a scheduling alias, and secure video; information shared only with her consent. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Marchetti-Osei, who saw her the same day. The diagnosis, the reasons for outpatient care, the admission thresholds and the plan were explained to Empress Elisabeth, who agreed to try outpatient treatment with the team. [S]
Follow-up: Psychiatry review by video at about four weeks, then as needed; CBT-E weekly; dietitian every two weeks. [S]
